9.1 Normal AC Power Systems 
 
Learning objectives: 
 
1. Recognize the purposes of the Normal AC Power system. 
  
2. Recognize the purpose of the following Normal AC Power system major 

components: 
a. Unit Generator and Auxiliaries 
b. Generator Output breakers 
c. Main Transformers (MT) 
d. Normal Station Supply Transformer (NSST) 
e. Reserve Station Supply Transformer (RSST) 
f. Gas Turbine 
g. 4160v Buses 
h. 480v Distribution system 
i. Generator Bus Duct Cooling System 
 

3. Recognize how power is distributed to the Normal buses from the: 
a. Normal Station Supply Transformer (NSST) 
b. Reserve Station Supply Transformer (RSST) 
c. Gas Turbine 

 
4. Recognize how the Normal AC Power system interfaces with the following systems: 

a. DC Power System (Section 9.4) 
b. Emergency AC Power System (Section 9.2) 

 
9.1.1 System Introduction 
 
The purpose of the Normal AC Power (NP) system is to provide adequate power to unit 
auxiliary loads for normal operation of the plant.  Two physically independent off site 
power supplies are provided to safety related loads supplied from the emergency buses.  
These two physically independent power supplies are from the 138KV and the 69KV 
offsite transmission systems. 
 
9.1.2 System Description 
 
The Normal AC Power system includes the following; 
• a Normal Station Service Transformer (NSST) 
• a Reserve Station Service Transformer (RSST) 
• a Main Transformer (MT) 
• 4160V buses 
• a 480V distribution system 
 
Both of the station service transformers are step-down transformers.  The NSST steps 
138KV down to 4160V and the RSST steps 69KV down to 4160V.  Each of the step-
down transformers has two secondary windings.   



 
Rev 09/11 9.1-2 USNRC HRTD 

 
The NSST normally supplies buses 1A and 11.  The RSST normally supplies buses 1B 
and 12.  Each of the transformers serves as a backup supply for the other.  Loads 
associated with the four 4160V buses are listed in Table 9.1-1. 
 
The Main Transformer (MT) is a step-up (24KV to 138KV) transformer.  The main 
transformer takes the output of the station turbine generator and supplies it to the NSST 
and the grid. 
 
Each of the 4160V buses supplies a 4160V to 480V step-down transformers for the 
480V distribution system. 
 
9.1.3 Component Description 
 
The major components of the Normal AC Power System are shown in Figure 9.1-1 and 
9.1-2 are discussed in the following paragraphs. 
 
9.1.3.1 Unit Generator and Auxiliaries 
 
The purpose of the unit generator is to transfer the mechanical energy from the main 
turbine into electrical energy. The rotating shaft of the main turbine is coupled to the unit 
generator's rotor.  The rotor supplies the rotating magnetic field necessary to produce 
electricity from the generator. 
 
The unit generator design ratings are as follows; 
• 1800 rpm 
• 820 MWe, 
• 978MVA 
• 60 Hz 
• 24KV. 
 
The output from generator is three phase AC power supplied to the grid and station 
loads.  Each phase output is routed through a specially constructed conductor which in 
turn is encased in a cooling duct.  The generator bus duct cooling system discussed in 
section 9.1.3.9. 
 
The unit generator has auxiliary support systems which are required for its operation.  
These support systems are discussed in the following paragraphs. 
 
9.1.3.1.1   Generator Gas System 
 
The generator rotor windings and casing are cooled by the circulation of hydrogen gas 
within the generator.  This gas is maintained at approximately 60 psig and greater than 
90% purity.  Hydrogen is used because it provides relatively low windage losses and 
good thermal conductivity.  Hydrogen removes heat at approximately seven times the 



 
Rev 09/11 9.1-3 USNRC HRTD 

rate of air while using less power to circulate the hydrogen gas.  Pressurizing the 
hydrogen gas to 60 psig increases its heat removal capacity.  The high purity 
requirements minimize the possibility of a hydrogen gas fire or explosion.  The gas is 
cooled by four hydrogen coolers .  These in turn are cooled by the turbine building 
closed loop cooling water system.   
 
9.1.3.1.2  Generator Hydrogen Seal Oil System 
 
A hydrogen seal oil system is used to prevent the hydrogen gas from escaping the 
generator.  Cool, clean oil from the turbine lubricating oil system is supplied to the 
hydrogen seal oil system storage tank.   The hydrogen seal oil system pumps then 
supply oil to the generator seals at 8 psig above generator gas pressure.  The oil from 
the seals flows back to the turbine lube oil system for cooling and cleaning. 
 
9.1.3.1.3  Generator Stator Cooling System 
 
High purity, low conductivity water is used to cool the generator stator bars and the 
exciter rectifiers.  Water is used because it has a high heat capacity and low viscosity.  
The electrical conductivity of water is kept to a minimum.  The water is continually 
filtered to reduce particles which could cause electrical shorting in the stator.  By 
maintaining conductivity less than 0.5 μmho/cm the stator bars are not shorted out by 
the water.  The stator cooling system heat exchangers are cooled by the turbine 
building closed loop cooling water system. 
 
9.1.3.1.4  Generator Alterex Exciter System 
 
The main generator excitation system is a GE Alterex system.  This system uses an 
auxiliary AC generator (alternator-exciter) as its power source.  This is required as the 
unit generator excitation power requirements are relatively large (1860KW and 500V).  
The alternator-exciter is driven by a direct coupling to the main generator rotor.  It is a 
three phase, 60 Hz, 4 pole, air cooled machine with it's output connected to a group of 
static rectifiers.  The static rectifies change the AC from the exciter to DC for application 
to generator rotor. The rectified DC output is applied to the generator rotor field 
windings via collector slip rings and brushes. 
 
 
9.1.3.2 Generator Output Breakers  
 
The main generator is supplied with two parallel generator output breakers.  The 
generator output circuit breakers are installed between the main turbine and the grid.  In 
the open position, the generator output breakers isolate the main transformer and 
generator from the grid.  Off site power from the grid is provided to the normal AC power 
system via the NSST.   
 



 
Rev 09/11 9.1-4 USNRC HRTD 

In the closed position, the generator is connected to the main transformer and provides 
power to the grid and normal AC power system.  The generator output breakers are 
high volume, double throw, oil filled circuit breakers.  The oil provides a high resistance 
medium between high voltage terminal points in the open position.  The purpose of the 
generator output breakers is to protect the unit generator and main transformer from 
electrical faults.  A list of the protective trips provided by the generator output breakers 
is listed in Table 9.1-2. 
 
The generator output breakers are used to synchronize the generator to the 138KV AC 
grid.  They are controlled from the generator section (MCB01-R) of the main control 
board in the control room.  Either generator output breaker may be used to synchronize 
the generator to the grid.  The generator output breaker to be used is selected by the 
synchronizing selector switch.  This switch connects the generator and the grid to a 
synchroscope and voltmeters.  When the first generator output breaker is synchronized 
(voltages and frequency matched) the operator closes the breaker.  The second breaker 
may then be closed after selecting it with the synchroscope.  The generator and grid are 
already in synchronization because the first generator output breakers is closed. 
 
9.1.3.3 Main Transformers 
 
There are two Main Transformers each consisting of three single phase, forced oil and 
air cooled transformers.  Leads from the unit generator are connected to the primary 
windings of the Main Transformers.  The high voltage grid leads are connected to the 
secondary windings.  The Main Transformers serve as step-up (24KV/138KV) 
transformers when the generator output breakers are closed. 
 
9.1.3.4 Normal Station Service Transformers 
 
The Normal Station Service Transformers (NSSTs) are step-down (138KV/4160V) three 
phase transformers.  The NSST supplies the following: 
• preferred power to nonsafety related 4160V system buses 1A and 11 
• preferred power to 4160V emergency AC system buses 101, 102, and 103  
• backup power to the 4160V AC system buses 1B and 12 
 
The primary winding is supplied by a 138KV connection to either the unit generator or 
the grid.  The NSST has two secondary windings.  Two windings are used for voltage 
transient separation while starting the Reactor Recirculation MG Set Drive Motors.  The 
NSST is the normal preferred power source for two of the four 4160V normal AC power 
buses and all of the 4160V emergency power system buses.   
 
The NSST is a nitrogen blanketed, oil/air cooled transformer.  The NSST is supplied 
with redundant protective relaying schemes.  This relaying isolates the transformer 
electrical connections in the event of an electrical fault condition.   
 



 
Rev 09/11 9.1-5 USNRC HRTD 

If the supply breakers from the RSST to the 4160V buses trip an automatic transfer to 
the NSST will occur.  This auto transfer will not occur if there is a bus fault 
 
9.1.3.5 Reserve Station Service Transformers 
 
The Reserve Station Service Transformers (RSSTs) are step-down (69KV/4160V) three 
phase transformers.  The primary winding is supplied by a 69KV connection to the grid.  
The RSST normally supplies the following; 
•  preferred power to nonsafety related 4160V system buses 1B and 12 
• back up preferred power to 4160V emergency AC power system buses 101, 102, 

and 103  
• backup power to the 4160V system buses 1A and 11 
 
If the supply breakers from the RSST to the 4160V buses trip an automatic transfer to 
the NSST will occur.  This auto transfer will not occur if there is a bus fault 
 
The RSST is also a nitrogen blanketed, oil/air cooled transformer.  The RSST has 
redundant protective relaying schemes to isolate the transformer in the event of an 
electrical fault condition.   
 
 
9.1.3.6 Station Gas Turbine 
 
The gas turbine acts as a reserve power supply for the 69KV distribution network and 
can be aligned directly to the RSST.  The gas turbine is not located on site. It is not 
designed to be switched into the 69KV distribution network in the loaded condition.  The 
gas turbine is controlled by a grid load dispatcher, not by the station operators. 
 
The gas turbine was designed as a safeguard against a total loss of site power (station 
blackout).  The addition of a third source of power to the normal AC power system 
makes a station blackout a very low probability. 
 
9.1.3.7 4160V Normal Power AC Busses 
 
There are four 4160V normal power system buses (1A, 1B, 11, and 12).  The normal 
power supply to buses 1A and 11 is the NSST.  The normal supply to buses 1B and 12 
is the RSST.  Buses 1A and 1B normally supply large motors only.  Buses 11 and 12 
normally supply smaller loads.  Typical loads supplied by the 4160V system buses are 
listed in Table 9.1-1.  The normal supply breakers to the 4160V buses are 2000 amp 
fast acting breakers.  The backup supply breakers have a 1200 amp capability. 
 
9.1.3.8 Normal 480V Distribution 
 
The 480V normal AC power system consists of eight metal clad switchgear buses.  
These are combined through a bus tie breaker into four double ended buses.  The 480V 



 
Rev 09/11 9.1-6 USNRC HRTD 

system buses are fed by 4160V normal AC power system buses 11 and 12.  Control 
power for the 480V switchgear is supplied by 125VDC.  A one line drawing is presented 
in figure 9.1-2. 
 
Power to the 480V loads is provided by Secondary Unit Substations (SUS).  A SUS 
consists of 
• a primary section for the connection to the 4160V circuit 
• a three phase transformer section from 4160V to 480V 
• a secondary section for the connection for 480V motors, power panels, and Motor 

Control Centers (MCCs).  
 
The transformers have a primary winding voltage of 4160V and a secondary winding 
voltage at 480V.  The transformers have automatically controlled forced oil and air 
cooling systems.  The SUS circuit breakers are normally electrically opened and closed.  
Manual operation is possible with control switches mounted on each SUS section.  
Each 480V normal bus and MCC can be energized from the opposite divisions 480V 
bus.  A bus tie breaker is closed if the normal power supply is or will become 
unavailable. 
 
The 480V motor control centers supply power to the following 
• small motors 
• motor operated valves 
• 120V lighting distribution panels 
• 120V power panels 
• battery chargers for the non safety 125V DC batteries 
 
Each MCC has various sized motor starters contained in cubicles on the motor control 
center.  The starter contacts open and close electrically to start or stop loads.  The MCC 
provides instantaneous protection for motors and time delay over current protection for 
feeds to power panels. 
 
9.1.3.9 Generator Bus Duct Cooling System 
 
The generator bus duct cooling system consists of one fan and its supporting 
equipment.  Air is discharged from the fan and passes through the generator bus ducts 
to remove heat.  The air is then passed through an air/water heat exchanger and then 
returned to the fan.  Cooling water is supplied by the turbine building closed loop cooling 
water system. The bus duct cooling system must be in operation to support generator 
outputs of greater than 45% load. 
 



 
Rev 09/11 9.1-7 USNRC HRTD 

9.1.4 System Features and Interfaces 
 
A short discussion of system operation and interfaces between this system and other 
plant systems is given in the following paragraphs. 
 
9.1.4.1 Normal Operation 
 
Under normal operating conditions, the normal power system supplies AC power to the 
equipment required for normal plant operation.  The turbine generator supplies power to 
the 138KV grid through the main transformer.  The NSST receives power from the 
138KV grid.  The RSST receives power from the 69KV grid and could receive power 
from an assigned gas turbine.  The RSST and NSST step the voltage down for use on 
the normal and emergency AC power system 4160V buses.  The voltage on the normal 
and emergency system 4160V buses is stepped down by the 4160V switch gear to 
480V.  This 480V power is supplied to eight normal AC system and three emergency 
power system 480V buses. 
 
9.1.4.2 System Interfaces 
 
The normal AC power system interfaces with virtually every plant system.  Table 9.1-1 
provides a listing of some of the more important loads supplied by the system.  Other 
important interfaces are discussed in the following paragraphs. 
 
DC Power System (Section 9.4) 
 
The DC Power System supplies control power to the high and medium voltage AC 
switchgears and circuit breakers. 
 
Emergency AC Power System (Section 9.2) 
 
The Emergency AC Power System is normally energized by the normal AC power 
System. 
 
9.1.5 Summary 
 
The normal AC power system provides power to unit auxiliary loads needed for normal 
operation of the plant.  Two physically independent off site power supplies are provided 
from the grid to the emergency bus safety related loads.  The two physically 
independent power supplies are from the 138KV and the 69KV grid.  The NSST and 
RSST both serve normal and backup preferred power functions.  The gas turbine 
provides an additional source of offsite power to the system. 
 
The normal AC power system has a quick transfer function which transfers loads from 
normal preferred power to backup preferred power.
